# {dplyr}

## `{dplyr}` ![](https://d33wubrfki0l68.cloudfront.net/621a9c8c5d7b47c4b6d72e8f01f28d14310e8370/193fc/css/images/hex/dplyr.png){fig-align="right" width="10%"} {.smaller}

A grammar for data wrangling (verbs!)

Take a couple minutes with your neighbor to guess what the following functions do:

* `select()`
* `filter()`
* `mutate()`
* `arrange()`
* `summarize()`
* `group_by()`

```{r, echo = FALSE}
countdown(minutes = 2, seconds = 00)
```

## `{dplyr}` {.smaller}

A grammar for data wrangling (verbs!)

`select()`

::: {.fragment}
a subset of **columns**
:::

`filter()`

::: {.fragment}
a subset of **rows**
:::

`mutate()`

::: {.fragment}
**add** a new column or **modify** an existing column
:::

`arrange()`

::: {.fragment}
**sort** rows in ascending/descending order
:::

`summarize()`

::: {.fragment}
a new column created according to other columns
for example: `mean()` or `sd()`
    + often used with...
:::

`group_by()`

::: {.fragment}
**grouping** categories in column(s)
:::

## Arguments

* **`{dplyr}` always takes a data frame (tibble) as the first argument**
    + just like `{ggplot}`

* subsequent functions tell `{dplyr}` what to do with the data frame

* each function applied returns the modified data frame

## `select()`

choose columns

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r, eval=FALSE}
data.frame |> 
  select(a, c)
```

## Examples

Let’s go back to the `penguins` dataset

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

library(tidyverse)
#install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins
```

## `select()` 

from `penguins`: `species` and `island` and `body_mass_g`

```{r, eval=FALSE}
select(penguins, species, island, body_mass_g)
```

. . .

**OR** more typically

```{r}
penguins |>
	select(species, island, body_mass_g)
```

## Negation `-`

Don't select (or drop) variable(s)

```{r}
penguins |>
	select(-year)
```

## Negation `-`

Don't select (or drop) variable(s)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins |>
	select(-bill_length_mm, -bill_depth_mm)
```

**OR** maybe better

```{r}
penguins |>
	select(-c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm))
```

## Indexing

Less preferable because variable orders change

```{r}
penguins |>
	select(1:3)
```

## Use multiple methods

```{r}
penguins |>
	select(species, 3, 5)
```

* `starts_with()`

* `contains()`
* `all_of()`
* `any_of()`

## Mix `select` methods and helpers

You can mix types and helper functions

```{r}
reads |> 
    select(student_id, 1, starts_with("total"))
```

## Mix `select` methods and helpers

You can also use select to rearrange your columns

```{r}
reads |> 
    select(student_id, 1, starts_with("total"), everything())
```

## `relocate()`

[relocate(]{style="color:#D55E00"}[.data]{style="color:#56B4E9"}, ... [.before = NULL]{style="color:#009E73"}, [.after = NULL]{style="color:#E69f00"}[)]{style="color:#D55E00"}

. . .

[.data]{style="color:#56B4E9"} = dataframe/tibble

... = columns to move

[.before]{style="color:#009E73"} = variable to move *before*

[.after]{style="color:#E69f00"} = variable to move *after*

- supplying *neither* [.before]{style="color:#009E73"} nor [.after]{style="color:#E69f00"} moves columns to the left-hand side by default
- specifying *both* is an error

## `relocate()`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins 

```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
penguins |> 
  relocate(year)
```
:::

::::

::: aside
moves "year" to far left (default)
:::

## `relocate()`

```{r}
penguins |> 
  relocate(year, .after = species)
```

::: aside 
moves "year" after "species"
:::

## `relocate()`

```{r}
penguins |> 
  relocate(year, .before = bill_length_mm)
```

::: aside
moves "year" before "bill_length_mm"
:::

## Let's remove these aggregate rows

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|4|5"
students_only <- reads |>
  filter(student_id != "All Students (Average)") 

students_only |>
```

## Not equal 

`!` means **NOT**

`!=` means **NOT equal**

Note:

- If you want values that are NOT `NA`:
    + `filter(!is.na(variable))`
    + ~~`filter(variable != NA)`~~

## Chaining `{dplyr}` functions

What if we wanted to `filter` then `select` a data set?

Select "*island*" and "*species*" of penguins over 4200 *grams*

. . .

(1) Two step method 😐

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|3"
#| 
penguins_big <- filter(penguins, body_mass_g > 4200)

penguins_big <- select(penguins_big, island, species)
```

## Chaining `{dplyr}` functions {.smaller}

(2) Alternatively, we could wrap `select` around `filter` ☹️

```{r}
select(filter(penguins, body_mass_g > 4200), island, species)
```

## Chaining `{dplyr}` functions

(3) Piping functions 🎉

We could use the pipe function to help increase the readability of our code: 
<br>
`|>`
<br>

Called the "pipe" operator and "piping functions"

```{r}
filter(penguins, body_mass_g > 4200) |> 
  select(island, species)
```

## Piping functions {.smaller}

Even better:

* Generally when using the pipe, the first argument is the data set, which gets piped through the corresponding functions
* So the code on the prior slide would be:

```{r}
penguins |> 
  filter(body_mass_g > 4200) |> 
  select(island, species)
```

::: aside
Note the lovely indentations and line breaks to help keep things straight! This is nice!
:::

## [`filter_out()`](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2026/02/dplyr-1-2-0/#expanding-the-filter-family)

Hot out the `tidyverse` factory!

. . .

- `filter()` is designed around supplying rules about which rows to **keep**
- We need a verb designed around supplying which rows to **drop**

Both `filter()` and `filter_out()` treats `NA` values as `FALSE` 

- `filter_out()` expects that you are going to tell it which rows to **drop**, so the default behavior of treating `NA` like `FALSE` works with you rather than against you

## Quick example

Filter out rows where the *patient is deceased* **and** the *year was before 2012*

```{r}
(patients <- tibble(
  name = c("Anne", "Mark", "Sarah", "Davis", "Max", "Derek", "Tina"),
  deceased = c(FALSE, TRUE, NA, TRUE, NA, FALSE, TRUE),
  date = c(2005, 2010, NA, 2020, 2010, NA, NA)
))
```

## What we think we want

```{r}
#| eval: false
patients |>
  filter(!(deceased & date < 2012))
```

. . .

But the result shows...

```{r}
#| echo: false
anti_join(
  patients,
  patients |> filter(!(deceased & date < 2012)),
  join_by(name, deceased, date)
)
```

We dropped rows with `NA` because we aren’t sure about the condition

We only should have dropped "Mark"!

## Correct with `filter()`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
patients |>
  filter(
    !((deceased & !is.na(deceased)) &
      (date < 2012 & !is.na(date)))
  )
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

![](https://media1.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExMjd0MGtneXY2emIxeHBjbGRxbzRnZHd1cmVsbzNoNWIydWs5Njc0OSZlcD12MV9pbnRlcm5hbF9naWZfYnlfaWQmY3Q9Zw/2ifaoMRd5w9jrsE7QK/giphy.gif)

:::

::::


## Better with `filter_out()`

```{r}
patients |>
  filter_out(deceased, date < 2012)
```

# `mutate()`

## Some new data

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
(prepost <- reads |> 
  filter(student_id != "All Students (Average)") |> 
  select(student_id, test_site, pre_test_score, post_test_score))
```

## `mutate()`

**Add** a variable

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"

prepost |> 
  mutate(gain = post_test_score - pre_test_score)
```

## 

```{r}
names(prepost)
```

. . .

Why do we not see the new *gain* column?

## `mutate()` {.smaller}

**Add** *multiple* variables...

Use a variable you just created!

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
prepost <- prepost |>
  mutate(
    gain = post_test_score - pre_test_score,
    sum_tests = post_test_score + pre_test_score,
    pct_tests = (sum_tests/180) * 100
  )
prepost
```

::: aside
Again, note the line breaks to help keep things straight! This is nice!
:::

## `mutate()`

**Change** a variable

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
prepost <- prepost |> 
  mutate(student_id = parse_number(student_id))
prepost
```

# `arrange()`

## `arrange()`

Order the data

- Order by "*gain*", ascending [default]

```{r}
prepost |> 
  arrange(gain)
```

## `arrange()`

Order the data

- Order by "*pre_test_score*" and "*gain*", ascending

```{r}
prepost |> 
  arrange(pre_test_score, gain)
```

## `arrange()`

Order the data

- Order by "*gain*", `desc`ending

```{r}
prepost |> 
  arrange(desc(gain))
```

## `arrange()`

Order the data

- Order by "*pre_test_score*" and "*gain*", descending

```{r}
prepost |> 
  arrange(desc(pre_test_score), desc(gain))
```

# `summarize()`

## `summarize()` {.smaller}

`summarize()` or `summarise()`

* Here: compute the `mean` and `standard deviation` of the gain scores
* What are we looking at?

```{r}
prepost |> 
  summarize(mean_gain = mean(gain, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_gain = sd(gain, na.rm = TRUE))
```

. . .

This is a good start for a descriptive table!

##

## `group_by()`

<b>Conduct an operation for each level of a grouping factor</b>

Here, compute the mean gain for each *test site*

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|3"
#| output-location: fragment
prepost |> 
  group_by(test_site) |> 
  summarize(mean_gain = mean(gain))
```

## `group_by()` {.smaller}

When you use `group_by()` and `summarize()`

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

You will get a row for each unique group

```{r}
mpg |> 
  group_by(cyl) |> 
  summarize(max_hwy = max(hwy))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

If you have multiple grouping variables, you will get a row for each unique combination of groups

```{r}
mpg |> 
  group_by(cyl, drv) |> 
  summarize(max_hwy = max(hwy))
```
:::

::::

## Add summarized column to full data

Use `mutate()`!

```{r}
prepost |> 
  group_by(test_site) |> 
  mutate(mean_gain = mean(gain))
```

## Retain only summarized columns

Use `summarize()`!

```{r}
prepost |> 
  group_by(test_site) |> 
  summarize(mean_gain = mean(gain))
```

## Pipe to `{ggplot}`!

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1,2,3|4|5|6"
#| output-location: fragment

prepost |> 
  group_by(test_site) |> 
  summarize(mean_gain = mean(gain)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(test_site, mean_gain)) + 
  geom_col(fill = "cornflowerblue", alpha = .7) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 

![](./images/kd.gif)

## Summarizing and Plotting

- Calculate mean *post_test_score* by test site

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|3"
students_only |>
  group_by(test_site) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(post_test_score))
```

## Plot it

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|1|3|4|5|6|7"
#| fig-height: 2.5

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 18))

students_only |>
  group_by(test_site) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(post_test_score)) |>
  ggplot(aes(test_site, mean)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8)
```

# A couple more verbs

`recode()` and `rename()`

## Recode with `ifelse()`

Recoding into dichotomous variable with `ifelse()`

`ifelse(`test, test == `TRUE`, test == `FALSE)`

*or*

`ifelse(`logical statement, do this `if` TRUE, `else` do this`)`

## Recode with `ifelse()`

Recoding into dichotomous variable with `ifelse()`

**Remember to pair with `mutate()`!**

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"
#| output-location: fragment
students_only |> 
  mutate(new_test_site = ifelse(test_site == "JONES", "district 1", "district 2")) |> 
  select(test_site, new_test_site)
```

## Recode with `recode()`

Recoding into multinomial variable

```{r, eval=FALSE}
recode(variable,
       old_category_1 = "new_category_1",
	     old_category_2 = "new_category_2",
	     old_category_3 = "new_category_3",
       ...
)
```

## Recode with `recode()`

Recoding into multinomial variable

**Remember to pair with `mutate()`**

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
students_only |> 
  mutate(test_site = recode(test_site,
                            JONES = "Jones Middle",
                            VIRDEN = "Virden Elementary",
                            WESTSIDE = "Westside High"
                            )
        )
```

## Recode with `recode()`

Remember to use backticks `` for special characters

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
mtcars |> 
  mutate(cyl_str = recode(cyl,
                      `4` = "cylinders4",
                      `6` = "cylinders6",
                      `8` = "cylinders8"
                      )
         ) |> 
  as_tibble()
```

## Recode with `case_when()` {.smaller}

Recoding across several variables, or if you find yourself using nested `ifelse()` statements

**Remember to pair with `mutate()`**

```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
#| code-line-numbers: "|6|7|8|9"

library(palmerpenguins)

penguins |> 
  mutate(species_big = 
           case_when(
             body_mass_g > 4500 & species == "Adelie" ~ "adelie_big",
             body_mass_g > 4600 & species == "Chinstrap" ~ "chinstrap_big",
             body_mass_g > 6000 & species == "Gentoo" ~ "gentoo_big",
             .default = "other"
           ))
```

. . .

`.default` equivalent to `all else`

## Recode with `case_when()` {.smaller}

~~`.default` equivalent to `all else`~~

`.unmatched = "error"` rather than `.default` and `case_when()` will error if that assertion doesn’t hold

This is great for defensive programming!

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment
#| error: TRUE

penguins |> 
  mutate(species_big = 
           case_when(
             body_mass_g > 4500 & species == "Adelie" ~ "adelie_big",
             body_mass_g > 4600 & species == "Chinstrap" ~ "chinstrap_big",
             body_mass_g > 6000 & species == "Gentoo" ~ "gentoo_big",
             .unmatched = "error"
           ))
```


## Recode some values

`replace_when()` is useful when you're updating an existing column and not mutating an entirely new one

```{r}
(pets <- tibble(
  name = c("Max", "Bella", "Chuck", "Luna", "Cooper"),
  type = factor(
    c("dog", "dog", "cat", "dog", "cat"),
    levels = c("dog", "cat", "puppy")
  ),
  age = c(1, 3, 5, 2, 4)
))
```

## Recode some values

Replace some `type` values with `"puppy"` based on certain conditions

```{r}
pets |>
  mutate(
    type = replace_when(type, 
                        type == "dog" & age <= 2 ~ "puppy")
  )
```

. . .

Easier to read with the pipe

```{r}
pets |>
  mutate(
    type = type |> 
      replace_when(
        type == "dog" & age <= 2 ~ "puppy")
  )
```


## `rename()` {.smaller}

`rename(new_name = old_name)`

**NOT paired with `mutate()`**

```{r}
penguins |>
  rename(
    home = island,
    bill_length = bill_length_mm
  )
```

## rename with `select()`

```{r}
penguins |> 
  select(species, home = island, bill_length = bill_length_mm, year) 
```



## Final notes on `{dplyr}`

* We could spend weeks on this
* We'll be using it all term long
* Verbs can help you gain fluency
* There are also conditional and all-inclusive versions of `mutate()`, `select()`, and `summarize()`

## [`across()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html)

Use `across()` to apply the same transformation to multiple columns

. . .

[across(]{style="color:#D55E00"}[.cols]{style="color:#56B4E9"}, [.funs]{style="color:#009E73"}, ...[)]{style="color:#D55E00"}

. . .

[.cols]{style="color:#56B4E9"} = columns to transform

[.fns]{style="color:#009E73"} = function to apply to each of the selected columns

## `across()`

Let's transform  the `penguins` columns in *mm* to *in* by dividing by 25.4

. . .

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins |> 
  select(ends_with("mm")) |> 
  mutate(
    bill_length_in = bill_length_mm/25.4,
    bill_depth_in = bill_depth_mm/25.4,
    flitter_length_in = flipper_length_mm/25.4
  )
```

## `across()`

Lets' do the same with `across()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column

penguins |> 
  select(ends_with("mm")) |> 
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("mm"), ~.x/25.4)
  )
```

- use helper functions to select columns
    + or `c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm)`
- `.x` is a placeholder for all 
- Keeps the same names


## `across()`

Same thing but let's change the names

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins |> 
  select(ends_with("mm")) |> 
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("mm"), ~.x/25.4, .names = "{sub('_mm', '_in', .col)}")
  )
```

## `across()`

Let's round some columns to the whole number

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins |> 
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("mm"), round)
  )
```

## `across()`

Let's round some columns to the second decimal

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins |> 
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("mm"), ~round(., 2))
  )
```

## `across()`

How about with `summarize()`?

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(across(c(bill_length_mm:body_mass_g), ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))
```

## `across()`

Let's add better names

```{r}
#| output-location: fragment

penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(across(c(bill_length_mm:body_mass_g), ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
                   .names = "mean_{col}"))
```
